subtopic: FOREST DESTRUCTION BY FUNGI AND INSECTS
FOREST DESTRUCTION BY FUNGI AND INSECTS
speechtext:
1.	Has the government any information relative to the amount of damage which is being caused in the forests of Canada and the industries related thereto; (a) by fungi; (b) by insects?
2.	Does such information relate to the forests under the jurisdiction of the Dominion Government and separately to the forests under the jurisdiction of the provincial governments?

3.	If so, what is the nature of the information whether in reports or otherwise and does such information disclose damages in percentage of trees destroyed or the value of the same?
4.	What steps, if any, are being taken to ascertain the extent of the losses due; (a) to fungi; (b) to insects?
5.	Has the government any men on the scientific staff or in the departments engaged in the study of the causes and control of damage caused by fungi and insects generally and if so, how many?
6.	How many men are engaged in the study of the causes and control of damage caused to forest trees; (a) by fungi; (b) by insects?
7.	Does the government consider such a staff sufficient to cope with the loss to such a great natural resource as the forests of Canada?
8.	Is it the intention of the government to extend the scientific study of the causes and control of damage and to take practical remedies for the preservation of the forests of Canada?

subtopic: FOREST DESTRUCTION BY FUNGI AND INSECTS
speechtext:
1.	(a) and (b). The government has a considerable amount of information with regard to insect injuries and fungi from many parts of the Canadian forest. This information has been collected by the division of Forest Insects of the Entomological branch and by the division of Botany of the experimental farms of the Department of Agriculture in cooperation with the Dominion Forestry branch of the Department of the Inte'rior and the various provincial forest administrations.
2.	This information relates to all Canadian forests wherever insects and fungous outbreaks develop and are studied.
3.	Information on injury caused by forest insects has been published in several bulletins and circulars by the Entomological branch of the Department of Agriculture and further information will be found in the annual reports of the Dominion Entomologist.
Information on fungous injuries will be found in the reports of the Dominion Botanist for the years 19^1 and 1922. Further detailed information concerning both these subjects is available in the files of the Department of Agriculture.
Records are kept of important forest insect and fungous outbreaks and detailed reports upon the injuries are prepared in all cases studied by our officers. These reports give the cause and course of the injury with its details and where possible the extent of the injury is determined, although accurate estimates of this kind are sometimes very difficult to obtain.
4.	(a) The division of Botany of the Experimental Farms branch conduct field examinations of forest areas with a view to ascertaining the damage due to fungi and the most feasible means of control. Extensive surveys have been conducted' in connection with the white pine blister rust in British Columbia and eastern Canada.

Questions
(b) In connection with all important forest insect outbreaks the officers of the division of Forest Insects in the Entomological branch conduct special forest insect surveys, often in co-operation with the dominion and provincial Forestry branches, in order to determine the cause and extent of the injuries. Extensive surveys of this kind have been made during the last two seasons in connection with the pine bark-beetle outbreaks in British Columbia and with the spruce budworm outbreaks in eastern Canada.
5.	The Entomological branch has 39 permanent technical officers on the scientific staff and provision is being made for 55 temporary and seasonal assistants this season.
The division of Botany has 14 permanent technical officers and provision is being made for 33 permanent and temporary assistants this season. All these officers are engaged in the study of the causes and control of damage caused by fungi and insects generally.
6.	(a) The division of botany employs one technically trained forest pathologist and in adition 6 temporary assistants are to be employed this summer.
(b) The division of forest insects in the Entomological branch employs 7 technically trained officers engaged solely in investigation of forest insects and their injuries and control. Five of these are stationed in eastern Canada and two in British Columbia. In addition these officers are assisted by permanent or seasonal assistants according to their need.
7.	The government is fully aware of the fact that as far as forest pathology is concerned, considerably more work should be done, and is ever ready to give careful consideration to the representations made by the industries concerned in order to assist in the solution of these serious causes of losses to our forest resources.
8.	The Entomological branch has extended its investigations of the dying balsam and spruce in eastern Canada, with a view to determining the cause and rate of deterioration of the dying and dead timber and the degree to which it can still be salvaged.
A great amount of work in connection with the natural control of spruce budworm by means of parasites bred and distributed from the entomological laboratory at Fredericton, N.B., has already been performed This work has now been placed directly under the charge of the division of forest insects. A report on past work in this connection has been practically completed and will shortly be published. A scheme of co-operation is also contemplated between the owners of some timber limits and the division of Botany
whereby the services of trained forest pathologists will be available for the particular study of various diseases affecting balsam and spruce in the eastern forests.

speakeroldname: Hon. A. B. COPP (Secretary of State):
speechtext: The suggestion made by my hon. friend for St. John City (Mr. Baxter) for the consolidation of our naturalization law was referred to the officials of the department. While many arguments might be advanced in favour of the consolidation of this and other legislation, owing to the fact that a very large number of forms have been already printed under the title of the present act, and would have to be scrapped if we proceeded with consolidation, involving a waste of something like $15,000 or $20,000, I do not think the advantage that would accrue from such consolidation would warrant this heavy loss, especially bearing in mind that the consolidation and revision of our Dominion statutes is under consideration and will be taken in hand within a very short time. Therefore it seems to me that we might very well defer the consolidation of our Naturalization law until the consolidation of our statutes generally is undertaken.

The reason given by my hon. friend for not bringing in a consolidated bill at the present session does not appeal to me as yery important. I remember that two or three years ago the same reason was given by the Under Secretary of State in relation to this same act-I think it was in 1919 when we were down in the old Museum building. This very bill was brought up and the question of consolidation of our naturalization law was objected to then on the ground that a lot of forms would have to be scrapped; and I think the Under Secretary of State had had new forms printed on that occasion. That does not seem to me to be a very substantial reason for postponing an absolutely necessary work if we are to understand our naturalization law as we should 
understand it. My hon. friend says that the work of consolidation has been considered, and I think he says it will be undertaken. I suppose he means in connection with the revision of the Dominion statutes. That work has been going on for some time, and I think we might reasonably expect it to be completed within the present year at all events. Therefore would it not be well for my hon. friend to allow this bill to stand in the meantime? _ No great injury and no great inconvenience will be suffered in the next few months by allowing this bill to stand until this consolidation takes place. He will agree with me, I am sure, that what he proposes now is a very radical departure from the practice in the past in regard to naturalization. I am satisfied that a good many members will desire to discuss the question, and as the session is fairly well advanced now for a measure of this kind, I would suggest that it stand over until a consolidated bill can be brought in and passed.

I should like very much to agree to my hon. friend s suggestion if I thought it would be in the best interests of the country and parliament to do so. He will remember that this bill was introduced last session after strong requests, amounting almost to demands, from different portions of the Dominion that some changes should be made in the act generally as well as in the administration of it. Under the conditions then prevailing I felt that we would be justified in allowing the bill to stand over until this session, but now it has gone forth that these amendments would be re-introduced and considered I think we should proceed with the bill. The amendments are only two or three in number. I agree with my hon. friend that in one particular instance the change is in a way somewhat radical, but I am sure that if he will give his attention to these amendments -and I know his legal knowledge and ability will stand him in good stead in doing so-he will * agree with me that they are desirable and will be of great advantage to all portions of the Dominion. After giving this matter my very best consideration, and after conferring with the officials of the department who have had charge of the administration of our Naturalization law long before 1914, I am confident that the suggested changes will be of very great advantage as affecting those who desire to become naturalized citizens of Canada. We open our doors to people from other lands; we give them to understand that our country is ready to receive them and that after residing in Canada a certain length of time they will be entitled to become aatur-

Naturalization Acts
alized Canadian citizens. So that with due inquiry as to their fitness, we should remove all annoying restrictions upon applications for naturalization. The suggestions I have made in this bill are of the simplest character and should, I am sure, meet with the approval of the committee.
Will the minister explain what the changes are?

I assume my hon. friend was not in the House the day before yesterday when I explained the proposed changes. I shall be glad, however, briefly to restate them. Prior to 1914 all applications for naturalization were made to the local judges of the courts in the different provinces. The application was presented to the court on the opening day and if no objection was made during the entire sitting of the court and the judge was satisfied that the applicant was a fit and proper person to become a Canadian citizen, the application was granted. In 1914 a change was made; it was provided that naturalization certificates should be issued, not by the judges of our courts, but by the State department. The applicant files his application with the clerk of the court, where it remains on file for three months. It is not published in any way; it may be hung in the clerk's office behind the door or the safe. At the end of three months, notice is supposed to be given to the applicant; he then appears before the court in person and the judge inquires into his qualifications for citizenship. Formerly the judge at this point had the decision in his own hands, but by the act of 1914, amended in 1920. it was provided that the judge should simply report to the Secretary of State whether he approved or disapproved of the application, and if the Secretary of State found the applicant to be a fit and proper subject for naturalization the certificate issued from the State department. My hon. friend, in discussing this matter the other day, suggested that it would be giving any minister very great power to leave wholly to him the decision whether or not applicants for naturalization should be given certificates. But by the present act, irrespective of the report made by the judges, irrespective of whether they approve or disapprove of the application, the Secretary of State has absolute discretion to say whether or not the application should be granted. In other words, I am taking no more power than we have under the present act, but I am asking that we do away with the provision under which a man's application is held up for three months while it is posted, perhaps, behind the door or elsewhere in the
office of the clerk. I do not suggest for a moment that the clerk would secrete it purposely, but there is no publication given to it and there can be no advantage in holding the application up in this manner for three or four months. The committee will agree that upon careful inquiry being made into his qualifications, it is our duty to give to an applicant for naturalization a reasonable opportunity of becoming a citizen of Canada without undue delay and that, so long as we provide reasonable safeguards, we should remove as many stumbling blocks as we can from his path.

What investigation
does the minister propose to substitute for the investigation that has been made by the county court judges? It is very necessary that someone should have the opportunity of coming in personal contact with the applicant. The minister says that the Secretary of State under the present law can issue a naturalization certificate irrespective of the report made by the county court judge. I suppose the minister would not suggest that the Secretary of State or the Under Secretary of State would completely disregard the report of the county court judge.
I believe that we should give naturalization to proper persons, but we should also safeguard the right to become a naturalized British subject because that right carries wdth it certain privileges which later on may become troublesome. We have had cases of that in British Columbia. We have found that naturalization certificates were issued without proper^ investigation. That was previous to 1914, and we have found since that time that naturalized British subjects who were improperly naturalized are demanding and insisting on certain rights to which they claim they are entitled because of their citizenship. I say it would be a great mistake to grant naturalization in a purely formal manner, long-distance naturalization, as it were, naturalization granted here in Ottawa perhaps three thousand or more miles away from the person who is applying for naturalization. I think the strictest kind of investigation should be made, and I submit, Mr. Chairman, that that investigation should be made by county court judges; I think they are eminently proper persons to conduct the investigation, and that they perform their duties in a very conscientious manner. I think it would be a great mistake for the Secretary of State at Ottawa, whether the present incumbent of the office or anyone else, to grant naturalization without some kind of personal examination of the applicant by some person who is qualified to

Is he going to take the recommendation of someone who says that the applicant is a fit and proper person to become a naturalized citizen of this country, or is he going to have a proper investigation made to see that the applicant is really entitled and is a proper person to become naturalized?

speechtext: Oh, the minister will answer the question.

I quite agree with the minister that three months is quite too long a time for an application for naturalization to be held up in the office of the clerk of the county court. It really does not give the general public any notice that application is being made because the general public does not visit the office of the clerk of the county court. But I cannot agree at all with the minister when he suggests that the investigation should be taken out of the hands of the county court judge and placed in the hands of an officer of the Mounted Police. If the minister is impeaching the integrity and the wisdom of the judges who are appointed by the Dominion government I would like him jto say so, but how any person can imagine that a member of the Mounted Police is more fitted to make an investigation as to the qualifications of a man to become naturalized than a county court judge I cannot possibly understand.
In our Niagara district we have very many foreigners from whom there is a continual stream of applications for naturalization. The notices are posted as the law requires, in the office of the clerk of the county court for three months. I say that is altogether too long, I cannot see the necessity for that length of time at all. What I would suggest is that a person who desires naturalization should go before a judge of the county court and be examined by him. The examination is not made in open court but in the jifdge's chambers. The applicant should submit himself to examination there, and if the judge of the county court reports to the Secretary of State that the man is entitled to naturalization, then he should become naturalized. That is a simple process, it is an inexpensive process, and it is a speedy process. If on

the other hand you have the investigation made by officers of the department, though I am quite sure that an officer of the department would make a very thorough and proper investigation, the investigation would be expensive, and you can see the time that would be lost if notice has to be sent to Ottawa and an officer of the department sent up there at the expense of the country to examine the applicant. Why should that expense be incurred when you have a judge of the county court there who is eminently capable of making the examination, is entirely impartial, and can make the examination at once?
To talk about an examination by an officer of the Mounted Police I submit is absolutely absurd. It is wrong; it should not be allowed. It is not even to be made by the officers; it does not say " officers ", it says by a member of the Mounted Police. I know that the Mounted Police is a very good, force composed of good men, intelligent men, but they are not by their training or their position fitted to make such an examination as is required in this case. I think it would be a great mistake if the department takes this examination out of the hands of the county court judges, who are appointed by this government. Let them reduce the time, let the investigation be made at once by a judge of the county court. He will make an impartial report, an intelligent, report, a report that will have the confidence of the people of this country.

In answer to my hon. friend for New Westminster (Mr. McQuarrie) who asked what we proposed to substitute for the investigation that is now held by county court judges, I would say that we do not propose to substitute any investigation for the investigation that is now made by the judges. From the experience we have had since this act has been in operation, the report from the judge is of absolutely no use to the department.
Why does the minister sai' that?
I will tell my hon. friend if he will have patience.
I have seen a good many examinations take place in court, and they are very thorough and reliable.

I have too. I do not say that all the reports are not of some use. The act under which we are now working, the act passed in 1914, for which I am not responsible, provides that this investigation is to be held

by the judge. Now from the reports we receive, the investigation that is held by the judges is not of such a character that the department which is charged with the responsibility of issuing the certificate can act upon it.
Why?

First, because the judges are only supposed to hold a very cursory examination under the act. Second, during the first years of the operation of this act the judges were paid for doing this work, and at the present time they are not being paid for doing it. That takes away a very great deal of the interest that the judges-for they are only human after all-might otherwise have in making the investigation if the whole responsibility were upon them. The Judges' Act precludes the judges from being paid any remuneration for doing this work, and under the act they realize that their examination and investigation is only intended to be cursory, and the report that is made by the judges contains a few remarks, approved or disapproved.
I would draw the attention of my hon. friend for South Simcoe (Mr. Boys), and my hon. friend for Welland (Mr. German) to this, that irrespective of the judge's report the same investigation has to be carried on by the department under the act. I appreciate the views my hon. friend holds and, to some extent, sympathize with him, because when this matter was first brought to my attention I thought it was a very proper thing to continue the investigation by the judge; but having had fifteen or sixteen months' experience in the administration of the act I find this procedure to be an absolute waste of time and of money. When the report comes from the judge we have to make a specific inquiry into the character and standing of the person -who had applied for naturalization. What do we do? We first apply to the Department of Immigration and we find out when the man entered the country, whether he entered legally, whether his name is on record at the port of entry, and whether he has been a resident of Canada long enough to become naturalized'.
The judge should find all that out.

He does not do so and the department has to get this information. We have to find out the character and standing o-reputation of the applicant during the time he has been a resident of Canada. In addition to making inquiry from the Department
of Immigration we may also conduct an investigation through the Mounted Police.
Are they scattered all over?
Yes.
In every province?

Yes. We also correspond with the local police, if necessary, in order to learn the required facts. Now, what I say to my hon. friend-and I think any legal gentleman will agree with me-is that in many cases a judge in a certain part of the province of Ontario, for example, after making an inquiry and examination will approve of an application, whereas a judge in another part of the country, with the same evidence before him, will disapprove of it. The department, as I say, makes this examination and inquiry and in many cases, notwithstanding that reports have come in from the judges approving of naturalization, we, after our own inquiry turn down the application and refuse to issue naturalization certificates. In other cases when the judges have sent in a report disapproving of the application of a man to become a British subject we, after careful inquiry, have been convinced that he is a fit and proper person to be naturalized and issue the certificate accordingly. Therefore, I contend that the time occupied in making this inquiry through the judge, under the law as it now stands, is absolutely wasted; the matter comes back to the department in the end. Such, at any rate, has been the experience of the department during the years that elapsed since 1914. The department must take the whole responsibility and it is entirely in its discretion to say whether the naturalization certificate should be issued or not.

If we are together in that, I cannot see how there is any room for doubt, because section 19 provides the procedure and says how it is to be done. There is absolutely nowhere else in Ontario that you can make application except to the Court of General Sessions. Now I want to make one observation regarding the procedure there. I am not going to suggest that the minister was saying anything derogatory of our judges. He may not know how they proceed in Ontario. I know something of the procedure in Ontario and especially in my own county. I have sat many times in the Court of General Sessions when these applications are made, and I want to tell the committee how it is done. The applicants are there in person. If that procedure is taken I cannot see how the minister can find fault with the decision of a judge. Does he suggest that in the province of Ontario the county judges frequently make reports which upon investigation the department disregard and reach a totally different conclusion? I can understand that might be the case in respect to outlying districts perhaps in the Northwest but I very much doubt if it is so in Ontario, and so far as that province is concerned I want to say to the minister I am satisfied from the care that is exercised in working out the provisions of this act that it would be unwise to make [DOT]a change so far as the older provinces of the Dominion are concerned. My hon. friend has argued that we have no jurisdiction when the report comes from the judge. That is true; I have never hinted anything else; that is our jurisdiction. But what I say is that under our law when the report comes from the judge to whom the application was made we can use our own discretionary power whether to accept that report or not.

Under what section is the
county court judge required to report if he is not in favour of naturalization? If he is not a fit and proper person a report does not reach your department.
Scores of them reach the department.

I would be glad if the minister would show me under what section a judge is required to make any report if his report is unfavourable. Section 23 is as follows-I need not take the trouble to read the previous sections which provide how the application is *o be posted, the opportunity for opposition, proof for qualification, and so on; when that is all done and the investigation has taken place, section 23 provides the next step, and what is it:
If the court decides that the alien is a fit and proper person to be naturalized and possesses the required qualifications, a certified copy of such decision shall be transmitted by the clerk of the court to the Secretary of State of Canada together with the application-
That is where the application is received.
-and such other papers, documents and reports as may be required by any regulation made hereunder.
The minister will see at once that the report only reaches his department when it is favourable. I do not say there is no other section, I do not profess to be an expert, but I ask the minister to show me any section which provides for transmitting a report when

it is not favourable. If there is no such section he would not hear of the matter unless the report is favourable.

Suppose the judge goes wrong in his law. That sometimes happens, not often, of course, but it has occurred, and he makes a report to the effect that this man has resided less than six years, when the law only calls for five, is the Secretary of State obliged to accept that report and refuse to issue a certificate?
He is under this act.
That would be absurd. That would be contrary to the law.

What I said was that a report would only reach the department when it was a favourable report. The judge may go wrong; they are all mortal; I am not saying they are infallible, but the point is the Secretary of State never hears of the application unless it is reported on favourably.
As I understand it, the report is sent forward.
I have asked the minister to show me the section. I am not saying it is not there; it may be; but let us see it. I have shown the section which provides for naturalization on a favourable report.
In the past fifteen months hundreds of applications have come forward from the judges marked "not approved".
But what difference does that make? These are beyond the purview of the act altogether.
If my hon. friend will wait just a moment. When that report is received it gives the Secretary of State authority to act under section 23.
Where is this section?
The Secretary of State acts upon the report. When that report from the judge is received it gives him authority to act.

There is where the minister is wrong, and I am sure that if he will consult his deputy he will find he is wholly wrong; there can be no question about it at all. The minister mentions that the practice is to get all sorts of reports as provided for by the act. Why, he may get letters from judges-all sorts of things. But only when he gets something which under the act empowers him to exercise his functions does he exercise them. Now the act says-in regard to the application coming through this
channel-that the minister's duty arises under the condition, and that one condition only, that under section 23 the judge sends a report that the man is a fit and proper person to become naturalized. The minister has the full discretion to act but he only has the discretion when section 23, and the other sections, are complied with; until section 23 is complied with he has no discretion whatever. Now, once his discretion arises he can say yes or he can say no, but he gets no discretion whatever until the judge sends in his report that the applicant is a fit and proper person. There is no lawyer-not even my hon. friend from George Etienne Cartier (Mr. Jacobs)- but would say the same thing; there is no other interpretation possible under this section.

Whatever may be the outcome of the legal discussion it would seem as if this amendment looks in the direction of more highly centralized authority, and very arbitrary authority at that. If I understood the Secretary of State aright the judge's report has no effect whatever in the final decision. If that is so the amendments placed before this House ought to look in the other direction altogether-that is towards very definitely giving the recommendation of the judges a place and weight in the final decision. I think it would be no less than an outrage if we allowed entrance to citizenship in Canada to be placed solely in the hands of one man. I am not reflecting in any way upon the present occupant of the office of Secretary of State-or on the occupant of that office any more than on the occupant of any other office-but it must surely be conceded that the question of whether or not a man should become a citizen of Canada ought not to be left to the absolute discretion of any one individual.
Further, the present legislation would seem not only to give this great power to one individual but it would also give to this same individual the right to disfranchise any citizen -a situation equally serious. According to the act of 1920:	,
The Governor in Council shall by order revoke a certificate of naturalization granted by the Secretary of State of Canada under this act, or granted under any Naturalization Act heretofore in force in Canada in any case in which he is, upon the report of the Secretary of State of Canada, satisfied that the person to whom the certificate was granted either-
(a) has, during any war in which His Majesty is engaged unlawfully traded or communicated with the enemy-	,
and so on. And
(c) was not of good character at the date of the
grant of the certificate.

Now it is obvious to anyone that it may be comparatively easy to say with regard to any particular citizen that he was not of good character five years previously. In that case, without any trial whatever, without any court coming to a decision on the matter in any form, the individual who has imagined himself to be a citizen of this country would thereby have withdrawn from him all the rights of citizenship. That, it seems to me, is an arbitrary power that is against all the ideas of British constitutional liberty that we have had in the past. To have made a change in that regard would seem to me to be something that might very well be brought before us at this time. But that provision still exists, and without any change in that particular clause we are being asked here to vote in favour of a further extension of this power to one individual.
But I would like particularly to call the attention of the House to the effect of this kind of provision and of this kind of procedure on the immigrant who comes to this country. We have tens of thousands of aliens scattered throughout the Canadian northwest. Many of them have come from other lands where they had exercised the rights of citizenship. They have been told that they could become free citizens of Canada. But for this they must wait five years-surely long enough. I should like, if I could, to get away from the official atmosphere of this House and ask you what effect it has upon these immigrants if, when they do make application for citizenship, they are treated more or less as though they were criminals, and mounted policemen sent around to investigate their character and their manner of life during the previous five years. There may be, it is quite true, an occasional criminal amongst them. I do not deny that; but I take it that we ought not in any sense whatever to regard prospective citizens as probably criminal. Surely the very essence of the British law is that a man ought to be regarded as innocent until he is proven guilty; he ought to be regarded as a good citizen until some definite charge is laid against him. Coming before the county court is a dignified proceeding. The people in the neighbourhood of the applicant's home have a chance of registering their opinion of his character. The judge is a man who is able, presumably, to give a disinterested opinion upon the evidence presented. There is no imputation whatever, there is no inference, that the applicant is anything but a desirable alien citizen honourably seeking to acquire citizenship in this new land. Any change in the procedure which would make it even possible

for the Secretary of State to send in an outsider to make inquiries among the neighbours of the applicant as to whether, possibly, he had done something that was wrong is a distinct lowering of the standard of citizenship which we ought to encourage in this country. For the sake of these tens of thousands of immigrants-many of whom those of us from the West know personally-I would ask that the citizenship of Canada should be placed on a higher plane; if so, I think that coming Canadians would, if necessary, gladly travel a hundred miles rather than submit to the inquisitorial methods proposed by these amendments.

I do not propose to discuss at all the technical questions which have arisen under the existing act. I am inclined to think that my right hon. leader has correctly interpreted that act. I only want to take the hour and a half or more that has been spent in trying to find out what a single paragraph of this act means as a text upon which to try, if I may, to emphasize to the House what I think was the wisdom of my suggestion the other day when this bill was before us, and that is that the measure should be reprinted and we should have here in one pamphlet exactly what it is intended the naturalization law of Canada shall be after this legislation is put through. We have spent an hour and a half debating as to what the present law may or may not mean, and I think I am not exaggerating when I say that there is not one individual here who is absolutely sure.
Several are absolutely sure.

All right, but they do not agree. I think this House will concur in the view that British citizenship is not a thing to be handed out like some cheap decoration, and that we do not want people coming to the shores of this country, with bombs in their pockets or criminal records, and being advanced by every possible sort of misguided sympathy to the status of Canadian citizenship.
They will have to carry the bombs in their pockets for five years.

They might find places of concealment. I think my hon. friend might show them places where they could conceal them for a time and then take them, if necessary, if there was an outbreak, for instance, in the city of Winnipeg.
The second point I should like to make is that while citizenship should not be given lightly to any one, the law ought to be so

Naturalization Acts
absolutely clear that there could be no room for misunderstanding either as to the conditions requisite for citizenship or the means to attain those conditions. I should like to see that in the bill. The other day I asked the minister if he would put in his bill the tribunal by which men are to be tried. Shall we have a branch of the Soviet, duly qualified to investigate people? Shall we go back to the days of the Terror and have a certain character of citizenship which will investigate the other citizens and demolish those who are unsatisfactory? Shall we have investigation by a secret police or by a judicial body? I look through this bill, and I do not find any clear-cut definition of what tribunal, by what means a man is to be adjusted to the citizenship which he proposes to assume. This is all left in the mind, in the discretion, in the magnanimity of the Secretary of State. That is precisely where I say it ought not to be. Judicial determination under the present system or the system of a few years ago, in my judgment-and I want to be frank and fair about this-was inadequate, because while I do not reflect upon the judges, while I think they did the best they could, there was not a dollar of the money of Canada spent, there was not the effort of a single official in Canada, as a sort of Crown proctor, to bring before them one solitary fact as regards the character of an applicant for citizenship. A man swore to formal affidavits; he presented himself before the court; he could be put through a certain cross-examination by the court, and the whole examination ended there. I think some of those who have gone on the roll of our citizenship might very well have tried to stand an inspection by members of the Royal Northwest Mounted Police or some other body accustomed to dealing with criminals. ' Many undoubtedly, got through who should not have had citizenship. I should like to see that feature of the act strengthened; but I will say on the other hand that it is not consistent with liberty, justice or fair play that the measure of a man's citizenship shall change from day to day and hour to hour according to, perhaps, the political exigencies of the gentleman who may occupy the position of Secretary of State. There is not in Canada a man who, when an election is not on, would do anything other than reprobate the idea of having a vast piece of political machinery that could be made use of at a critical moment. It is not the government that makes 5 p.m. citizens; it is ourselves who make them. We admit them to confraternity with the rest of us. Give the people, through some sort of judicial institution, an
opportunity of saying who is to be admitted to the brotherhood and who is to be excluded. But if the principle of this bill, if there be a principle in it, be adopted, we shall have either the knowledge of the law possessed by the gentleman who may be Secretary of State for the time being or his principal adviser, whoever he may be, or we may have the ignorance of the law, if unfortunately either of them should be succeeded by people who do not know the law. But whether it be knowledge or ignorance, what that department pronounces will be law, even though this parliament never enacted it, if we are to depend on government by order in council, by regulations made by the Secretary of State, by any Secretary of State, no matter how good a man he may be. What I am asking is that there should be written plain and large in the statute every condition that is necessary to enable the man to enter upon British citizenship, both the qualifications and the procedure. To find out this to-day, you have to go through four Canadian statutes and three Imperial statutes; it is necessary to refer from one to another. I ask that they be brought into this chamber, written together as they are to be acted upon, so that if an election was coming on A.B. can get the information he wants if he goes to some person interested in elections and says: "Can I vote? I was bom under certain conditions, in the United States or a foreign country. My father was a British silbject," and so on. "Have I a right to go on the roll? Can I swear that I am a British subject?" Hon. members have heard the discussion that has taken place this afternoon as to the powers of the Secretary of State. I have looked into the statutes to some extent, and I can assure the committee that the rest is as big a jumble with regard to the qualifications of a British subject as the bill is with regard to the powers of the Secretary of State. The Secretary of State will say that his powers are clear; other hon. members will say that they are not clear. Is that the condition of affairs we want to have when a man seeks to know on the eve of an election, simply whether he is or is not a British subject? This can be cleared up if we can get a comprehensive bill embracing all phases of the subject. We could get through a bill of that kind in a few hours, in less time thaD it has taken us to discuss what may or may not be the law. I asked for that the other day. It has been refused by the government on the ground that some thousands of dollars have been spent for forms. I should like to know this, and perhaps the Secretary of State will tell me: Was the government so sure that

this bit of legislation would be adopted by this House; were the view's that might be expressed by the rest of us with regard to this legislation so trivial.and of so little concern that it was not worth while waiting for us to have a chance to express our opinions, but that a button was pushed, the Printing bureau began to operate and tjiey got out tens of thousands of dollars worth of forms, saying that there would be a merely formal registration in this parliament because the minister was bringing down a bill? If so, do we count for very much here?
I think the hon. member has misconstrued the remarks I made.
Practically everybody seems to have done so.

I did not say that the printing was done because of the amendment I was introducing to-day. I said the printing was done because of the acts wre have in force and if this was changed-it is not the amendment I referred to-

I will accept the reason which is the most compelling reason for letting this amendment stand until the forms are used up. Either we are at such an emergency that, in order to save our citizenship, we have to make a new law, and if we have to do that we must waste the forms; or if we have not the emergency, we can wait a while and use up the forms. This legislation would do quite as well next year. J have no personal motive against it; I am quite willing to help as far as I can in devising something that will be workable and fair and that will at the same time be a protection to our citizenship. But I ask that it all be made plain to the people who have to act under it and to the people who have to invoke its assistance. By to-day there could have been a print of all the acts, and put together; we could have had that on every desk, so that we could see what the law will be when the minister gets it through. You cannot tell by these references what it will be.
I am going to point out one simple thing. If hon. members will look at the bill, they will see on the right hand page of the bill what professes to be a summary of the British Nationality and Status of Aliens Act, 1922. It is said that the sections we are asked to adopt are a reprint. Section 6 of the proposed bill is very nearly a reprint of section 3 of chapter 44 of the act of 1922 of the Imperial parliament. I do not like to have to deal with a technical matter of this sort because it is a little difficult to make it clear

to the House. But if the House will have patience I will read one clause which, in copying the Imperial bill, my hon. friend has absolutely omitted. The clause is this:
A copy of the principal act, with the amendments, whether by way of substitution, addition or omission required by this act, shall be prepared and certified by the clerk of parliament and deposited with the rolls of parliament; and his Majesty's printer shall print, in accordance with the copy so certified, all copies of the principal act which are printed after the commencement of this act.
There was the way they dealt with the matter in Great Britain, so that the people would have in one pamphlet the entire naturalization law. The Secretary of State told me the other day that his department would compile a pamphlet. I said I did not want a pamphlet made up by someone who was interpreting the law; I wanted a pamphlet that would reproduce, word for word, the law as this parliament makes it. Then if I have a view with regard to it and someone else has a different view we can go to a court and get the question straightened out. But if we have to act on the view of the Secretary of State or his deputy or anybody else we are simply bucking against bureaucracy and order in council government. I do not know whether it is one of those figments of the imagination in which we sometimes indulge, but I had thought that it was one of the claims of the Liberal party that they were opposed to order in council and bureaucratic legislation. I thought I had heard it repeated on many platforms that the business of parliament should be done here. I thought I heard my right hon. leader (Mr. Meighen) not only criticized but condemned, damned I might say everlastingly, because he ruled the country by order in council. But I do not find any great abatement of order in council government since the accession to power of my hon. friends opposite, and I find in this bill an absolute determination to put at the will of one man all the rights of citizenship in Canada and to do that by order in council and order in council only, without giving any necessary notice to the people whose rights are to be affected. If the House and the country want that sort of thing all they have to do is to take it; but I urge the members of this House to impress upon the minister that he either allow this legislation to stand over until next session or let it remain in abeyance for forty-eight hours at least until we can make a compilation of the statutes ourselves so that we may know what the legislation will be when the minister gets it into the shape in which he wants it. It has been utterly impossible since the bill was in-

Cold Storage Act
trodueed, unless a naan devoted his whole time to its consideration-and it would take half a day to go through the seven or eight or nine statutes that are all interlaced-to be able to form any kind of definite opinion as to what the law will be, unless we want to leave it in the pure, sheer ambiguity of order in council and the will of one individual who may be responsible at certain times only to party exigencies. The question for the country is this, I think: Shall naturalization be a matter of judicial determination upon a clear-cut, sane, well-known basis, open for every man to understand, or shall it be a matter of internal administration with the possibility of misuse for political purposes?

My hon. friend has made a
number of suggestions and I was very sorry I could not see my way clear to accept the one he offered the other day in regard to the consolidation of the acts. He has made another suggestion to-day, asking for forty-eight hours in which to go over the various statutes himself and come to a conclusion as to what the law really is in regard to naturalization. I have a good idea of the law myself so far as I have been associated with its administration, but I would draw my hon. friend's attention to the fact that this parliament has for very many years, and with a great deal of reason and advantage, followed the acts of the Imperial parliament. And this is the exact form which the naturalization law takes in Great Britain; the application is made directly to the Home Secretary who makes an investigation and either grants or refuses the certificate. I am still convinced that the situation as I have outlined it is proper. I can quite understand a number of legal gentlemen at first blush being somewhat apprehensive of taking this matter from the purview of the judges; I was of the same frame of mind myself when the proposal was first made. But when I considered the matter thoroughly I came to see the very great advantage that must and would accrue if the system now proposed were adopted. However, this is not a matter of life and death, and there is no imperious necessity to dispose of it either to-day or to-morrow, or within forty-eight hours. I am quite willing to have hon. gentlemen thoroughly consider it. and indeed I should be glad to have them do so. I am prepared to let it stand over for forty-eight hours as my hon. friend suggests.
Make it six months.
Well, that is hardly possible. I will therefore move that the committee rise and report progress.
Why not codify the law so that we could understand it?

My hon. friend is taking me literally in regard to my suggestion as to the length of time we might have to consider the matter; I hardly think that forty-eight hours would be adequate. Could we not have a reprint of the law as it will be in its final form so that we might have it all before us?
I will try to get that.
Thanks very much.

Will the minister be kind enough to see that a return is made to the questions I asked some time ago in re- [DOT] gard to the correspondence between the Secretary of State and the county court judges of Vancouver on the question of naturalization? I should like to have that information before me before we resume consideration of this matter.
To what is my hon. friend referring?
A motion was passed some weeks ago for a return of correspondence between the Secretary of State and the county court judges of Vancouver with reference to the question of naturalization.
I shall be glad to see that the return is brought down.
I desire to have it before this matter is proceeded with.

With reference to the question of naturalization certificates being issued on the authority of the judges, I would call the attention of the committee to a statement made by Judge Grant of Vancouver on the subject. He said that, "as long as I sit here as a judge I will always place the responsibility of granting naturalization on the Secretary of State and the government." When a member of the bench, who enjoys the respect that Judge Grant does, declares that he will always place the responsibility for granting naturalization on the government, I think that statement should go a long way to convince us that the Secretary of State is responsible for the citizenship of Canada; and if he is responsible I do not see why we should not leave the matter in his hands.
Progress reported.

Any person violating any provision of this act or of any regulation thereunder, shall be liable on summary conviction to a fine not exceeding four hundred dollars, or to imprisonment for a term not exceeding three months, or to both fine and imprisonment.
This is the provision for penalty. It is often the case that individuals in the West will send four, five or six carloads of stock from one farm or co-operative shipments may be sent forward and are handled by a commission firm, the sum involved in each case being some $5,000 or $6,000. It seems to me that if an individual wished to transgress the law he could appropriate thousands of dollars and $400 would be a very small penalty indeed. If a man wished to be crooked or deal unfairly, and took five or six or ten thousand dollars, he would willingly pay his $400. I think that penalty might be increased.

This precaution is in addition to the bond that he already has to give.
Section as amended agreed to.
On section 12-Regulations:

When the bill was in committee paragraph (d) was discussed from many angles and the article of wool was in
one day and out the next. It is in now and since the bill came from the committee representations have been made to the department by members of this House indicating that in so far as imported wool is concerned it is physically impossible to grade it, and therefore what is the use of including it here? It was pointed out that it was brought in in large bales rendering it impossible to be inspected or graded, and as it was bought by the one intending to use it, it was consequently a matter between him and the shipper. I think, therefore, that the word "wool" should . be deleted wherever it occurs in paragraph (d) as being an embarrassment to the importer and of no good to anyone else.
I would move, Mr. Chairman, that paragraph (d) be amended by striking out the word "wool" in lines 31 and 35.
Amendment agreed to.

I move to amend paragraph (f) to read as follows:
The manner in which calves are to be subjected to ante-mortem inspection, and the manner in which calves condemned by inspectors shall be disposed of.
Amendment agreed to.

Before this section carries, I believe the hon. member for Victoria City (Mr. Tolmie) had something to say in connection with it. He is not here just at the moment. Has the minister considered the conflicting sections between this act and the Animal Contagious Diseases Act with respect to meats and some other things.
Oh yes, we have had that under consideration.
Are the provisions of the Animal Contagious Diseases Act or the operations under that act, wherever they conflict with this act, to prevail?
We have taken precautions to see that they do not conflict.
What precautions?
In the drafting.
How do you distinguish between meat under the Animals Contagious Diseases Act and meat under this act?
Which subsection does my hon. friend refer to?

I refer to the paragraph in the interpretation clause:	.
"Live Stock" means meat cattle, sheep and swine and poultry.
Live Stock Acts

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I might point out we are on section 13 now. Section 2 was passed a very considerable time ago.

We have not passed section 12 yet, and section 12 purports to give power to the Governor in Council to regulate these things by order in council. It deals with the procedure, which is the vital thing. It may be that an inspector under the Animal Contagious Diseases Act would be carrying on his duties and another inspector under this act would authorize and pass out of the stockyard certain stock, and that when that stock . gets one hundred and fifty miles out the inspector under the Animal Contagious Diseases Act suspects it of some disease. Whose authority would prevail in that case?

These two inspections have an entirely different purpose in view. With regard to the Canned Meats Act the inspection is primarily from a sanitary standpoint The inspection under this act is for the purpose of determining the quality of the meat; not its sanitary character. The two do not conflict in the least degree. I think the hon. member for Victoria City (Mr. Tolmie) was quite satisfied with this when it was in committee.

He was not satisfied last evening when I was discussing the matter with him. I do not think the minister has really answered the question. The point is this. He says that under this act it is a question of quality that the inspector passes on. Now under the Animal Contagious Diseases Act it is a question of disease. In what way are the duties of these inspection departments to be co-ordinated so that they will not both be working on an animal at a certain time, and in order that both can carry on their duties conveniently?

I do not think their duties will conflict. Even under the Canned Meats Act, if I remember rightly, the inspection of the carcase is sufficient. When it has been inspected and approved by the officers of the department after the animal is slaughtered, it is recognized as being all right for canning purposes. It is entirely a question of quality of grade, if you like to call it that as to whether the meat is fit for caning purposes.

Is it not possible to have some system of inspection under which there will not be any confusion between two separate departments?
IMr. Ladner.]
Does my hon. friend mean separate branches of the same department?
Yes, certainly.

There has been
some conflict but owing to friendly co-operation there has not been any friction in the past. Sometimes there has been overlapping, to some extent but we generally overcome that by working in as amicable a manner as possible and there has been no particular friction.

I believe there is sometimes lack of co-operation, and there comes a time when the authority of the inspector who has to deal with diseases might conflict with the authority of the inspector under this act. Under those circumstances I submit that the authority of the former should prevail.

I think the hon.
gentleman is quite right. If there is any conflict of authority the question of sanitation should receive the first consideration. If my hon. friend has any suggestions to make I would be very glad to receive them and see whether they can be incorporated in the act.

I think the minister and myself agree on that point. Now, is there any provision in the act-if not one will be suggested-whereby there can be no difference in interpretation as to who has the authority? If so what is the provision in question?
Do you mean that there should be a provision of that nature in the act?
Certainly.
We will consider the proposition and see whether anything of that nature is required. In the meantime we can leave the bill in committee.

In this connection I think that every possible effort should be made to guard against any clashing of authority. The authority as between the two branches- the live Stock branch and the Health of Animals branch-should be quite clear and well defined. Let me point out the importance of that. In the event of an outbreak, or even a suspected outbreak, of disease in any of the live stock yards throughout the country any clashing of authority might result in very serious loss to Canada. Take for instance the outbreak of foot and mouth disease which occurred in the United States in 1914. Here there was a slowness in

Live Stock Acts
diagnosis, a clashing of state and federal authorities with the result that before they got through the disease had extended to some twenty-two states, with a loss of $20,000,000 to the country. It was with a view to avoiding anything of that kind that I think the authority as between the Health of Animals branch and the Live Stock branch should be clearly defined. In the case of disease, or suspected disease, the Health of Animals branch should be able to step in at once and take control and in that way prevent, perhaps, very serious loss to the live stock industry of the country. This is particularly important because we have an understanding with the United States under which we have worked very amicably for a number of years. An outbreak of foot and mouth disease in this country* would mean the quarantining of the American ports against our live stock, and, possibly, would also tie up our export overseas. The committee will readily realize how important this work is. I was upstairs preparing an amendment to this bill and had I got down in time should have moved it. I had no idea the bill was coming up quite so soon. However, I will be glad to let the minister have a copy. I will read this amendment which I desire to have added at the end of the bill. It is as follows:
18A. Notwithstanding the provisions in this act or any other act or law pertaining to or relating to live stock or in'connection with live stock yards, it is hereby enacted that in every case where in the opinion of -a veterinary inspector duly appointed in accordance with the provisions of the Animals' Contagious Diseases Act, a contagious disease or contagious diseases of animals exist, or are suspected to exist, the Animal Contagious Diseases Act and amendments thereto and the provisions therein shall prevail as against this act or all or any other act or acts relating to or pertaining to live stock or live stock yards as defined herein.
That will come in at the end of the bill-is that the idea?
That is the idea.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Section 12 is carried.
On section 20-Repeal:

I wish to make some further reference to the matter of penalties. The minister, in reply to the illustration which T gave, said that commission men were always bonded. That is true but the fact of their being bonded has not prevented them from infringing the act in the past. If a commission man has acted improperly in a case where money has been entrusted to him in the past the imposition of a paltry fine of four or five hundred dollars is not likely to act as a serious deterrent in the future

What the hon.
gentleman says is quite correct but in our commercial relations with each other we have always to take a business risk. Now, this risk has been been reduced to a minimum-first by requiring a bond and second by the precaution of opening a special account. There is also the penalty which has been referred to. If my hon. friend has any suggestions to make looking to further precautions I will be glad to discuss the matter with him. What can we do beyond enacting the provisions set forth here? The man is bonded; he is restricted as to the disposition he will make of the money entrusted to him; if he violates the law he is fined. We might provide a further punishment, we might hang him, but that would not help the man who lost the money any more than would the imposition of a fine. I will talk the matter over with the hon. member for Assiniboia and see if any further provision can be made to secure the owner of the cattle against further losses. There have been losses in the past. There is no question but that very considerable loss has taken place, and we want now to adopt safeguards as adequate as human ingenuity can suggest.

It is not my intention to ask the minister to hold the bill in committee; I think he understands the circumstances of the case thoroughly well. As I have stated, there have been these occurrences in the past; there is a possibility of their being repeated. The tendency of producers in the West is to go more and more into co-operation in the shipment of cattle. Instead of the carloads that formerly were shipped, there will be whole train loads going forward. It is not a question of a shipment valued merely at $1,000; the amount now involved runs into $10,000 or $20,000. I think the penalties in this case should be increased. The fine might remain at $400 but there should be a maximum, say, of $1,000; and the security should be on a graduated scale proportionate to the liability which rests on the commission man.

As I have already intimated we will leave the bill in committee for the present. My attention has been drawn to the further fact that in addition to the precautions contained in the bill, and the fact that an offender can be fined, there is this further fact that he can be expelled from the exchange, so that the offence cannot be repeated. But that does not meet my hon. friend's representation, nor do I think it can be met if we undertake to increase the bond from $10,000, because this would

simply increase the cost to the commission men that much more. I will, however, look into the matter to see whether the bond can be raised to advantage without embarrassing the trade generally.
